# Magic System {#sec-chapter-magic-system}

```{=typst}
#label("sec-chapter-magic-system")

#pagebreak()

Let's get one thing straight before we start: magic in this game always fires. Always. There is no spell slot to spend, no mana pool to drain, and no round where your best trick is already gone. When you cast, the magic happens. Your fire burns until _you_ decide it stops. The only question is how hard.

That changes how a caster plays. Every round you have something worth doing, and whatever you choose will leave a mark.

#pagebreak()

== Always Fires: The Core Rule

You don't roll to cast. You roll to determine _effect strength._ The spell goes off. The magic flows. Your 3d6 roll tells you whether the result is a sputter, a blast, or an inferno.

Every spell in this game has three outcomes built right into its stat block:

- *Weak:* The spell fires but underperforms. The firebolt singes instead of ignites. The heal knits flesh but leaves a scar. You got the job done, barely.
- *Standard:* Clean, expected result. Professional spellwork. This is what the spell was designed to do, and you did it.
- *Strong:* The magic surges. Extra damage, bonus effects, wider areas. The spell doesn't just work, it _dominates._ This is why you became a caster.

One roll. Three outcomes. No separate casting check and no spell failure percentage. Holding an ongoing spell is the one thing that asks for more, and the Concentration rule in Limitations covers it.

*Arcane spells* roll 3d6 + Knowledge + relevant skill. *Divine spells* roll 3d6 + Reason + relevant skill. Read the result. Magic happens.

#pagebreak()

== Spell Cards

Every spell above the cantrips is its own card. A spell family runs Novice, Adept, and Master, and each tier is a separate card with its own name and its own price. You buy the card you can afford and qualify for, and it never changes. That's the Ember Lance family in the table below: the Novice card Ember Lance, the Adept card Pyre Needle, and the Master card Smoldering Wake. The card carries its Disciplines requirement, Action, Range, and Keywords, then its effect. A Novice active card prints Weak, Standard, and Strong outcomes; an Adept or Master card prints a single Effect line.

A card is bought at one of three tiers, and the tier sets both the cost and the effect row:

You buy a card at its tier and you own that card. There is no rung to climb and no upgrade to pay for: the Adept and Master members of a family are separate cards with their own names and their own prices. Discipline ranks are bought separately, at your class's rates. See @sec-damage-budget for where those three rows come from.

#pagebreak()

== Level Gates and Disciplines

Every card has a *level gate* set by its tier: *Novice cards at level 1, Adept cards at level 3, Master cards at level 7.* The tier is a property of the card itself, not a count of its Disciplines. A Novice card can ask for several Discipline ranks, and an Adept card with no Discipline on its header asks for none.

On top of the level gate, a card requires the Disciplines printed on its header. Meet those ranks and you can buy the card. Want to throw Brimstone Burst? You need 2 Fire. Want its Adept sibling, Sulphur Aria? You need the same 2 Fire, plus level 3. See @sec-chapter-disciplines for the full rank and cost rules; every class sheet prints its own cost structure.

One ceiling still holds: *no single Discipline may go past rank 3.* The ranks follow the Discipline ladder (three different, two plus one, or all three the same), so a Master spell may blend types, fire and earth working together, or commit fully to a single force. This keeps Master spells a mark of earned mastery, broad or deep, never shallow repetition.

There are no wildcard Discipline substitutions, with one carve-out. Every Discipline requirement must be met with the specific Discipline named on the card, unless a class signature says otherwise: the Odd's *Eccentric Spellcasting* waives the prerequisites for two chosen abilities, one arcane and one divine, while the level gates still apply.

Three cards, one spell. Ember Lance is the Novice version: a tool. Pyre Needle is the Adept version: a weapon. Smoldering Wake is the Master version: an _event._ The level gate and the Discipline rank make sure you earn each step, but they don't make you wait half a campaign to take it.

#pagebreak()

== Cantrips

Cantrips are the spells you learn before you learn "real" spells. Minor magic. Parlor tricks that grew teeth.

Cantrips require *no Discipline prerequisites*, and they are free. Every caster knows the whole cantrip list for their tradition without spending a single DP on it. These are your at-will abilities, and each tradition has its own full list (see @sec-chapter-arcane-spells for arcane, @sec-chapter-divine-spells for divine). Small effects, infinite uses. When a cantrip's outcome actually matters, roll it like any other spell: 3d6 plus Knowledge or Reason and a relevant skill, then read the Weak, Standard, or Strong line.

Cantrips sit outside the damage budget. The budget keys damage to tier, and a cantrip has no tier: no Discipline prerequisite, no DP cost, and no rank to buy up. A cantrip's damage line is 1/3/5, deliberately below the Novice row, because a free at-will effect should never hit as hard as a card you spent DP on. See @sec-damage-budget

They won't win a fight. They'll start one, or end one creatively.

#pagebreak()

== Arcane vs. Divine Magic

Two traditions. Two philosophies. Same engine underneath.

*Arcane* (Arcanist, Odd, Unbalanced): Fire, Wind, Water, Earth, Energy, Mind, and Plants spells. Arcane casters manipulate natural forces through study, talent, or sheer force of will. They're scientists of the impossible, or artists of the unstable. Damage is their language. Destruction is their punctuation.

*Divine* (Shepherd, some Leaders): Protection, Animal, Life, Religion, and Plants spells. Divine casters channel power from a higher source, gods, nature, ancestors, the light between stars. They heal. They ward. They burn what shouldn't exist, like undead and demons. Their magic is a relationship, not a formula.

Some classes blur the line. The Odd steals from both traditions. The Unbalanced channels opposing elements through their own body. *Plants* answers to both sides, one Discipline behind an arcane venom and a divine briar alike. The game doesn't build walls between arcane and divine, it just asks what you're willing to pay.

#pagebreak()

== Limitations

Magic is powerful. That's the point. But there are brakes. Not to frustrate you, to make your biggest spells feel like _moments._

*Per-Encounter:* Adept and Master spells can only be used once per combat. You can't drop Sulphur Aria every round. Choose your moment. Make it count.

*Per-Session:* Master-tier spells are once per session. When you unleash Smoldering Wake or another Master card, the table should go quiet. These spells reshape encounters. They're not your default attack, they're your signature. Use them when it matters most. This is the tighter of the two limits: a Master spell does not come back in the next fight of the same session.

*Concentration:* Some ongoing spells, illusions, wards, enchantments, require concentration. You can only maintain one concentration spell at a time. If you take damage while concentrating, make a Fortitude check: *Standard or better* on 3d6 + Fortitude holds the spell together, and you make that check again each time damage lands on you. Concentration is about focus. Lose focus, lose the spell.

#callout(type: "note", title: "Why Limits on Master Spells?", body: [
I've seen what happens when a caster can drop their biggest spell every round. Combat becomes a fireworks display with no tension. The Blades and Protectors might as well put their dice away.

The per-session limit on Master spells isn't about counting resources. It's about who gets the spotlight. A Master spell should be the thing your table argues about on the drive home, and that only works while it stays rare.

The Veteran Adventurer
])

#pagebreak()

== Worked Example: Casting Sulphur Aria

Sera Ashvein is the party's Arcanist, a fire-obsessed scholar. By level 3 she has 2 Fire and 1 Energy, and Sulphur Aria is the spell she bought the moment the Adept gate opened. Now she's facing a cluster of goblins huddled behind a barricade. Time for a Brimstone Burst.

*The roll:* Sera's Knowledge is +2, and her Arcana is Novice (+1). The goblins are packed tight, Standard difficulty, no modifier. She rolls 3d6: 5, 3, 4 = 12. Plus 2 (Knowledge), plus 1 (Arcana) = 15. _Strong._

*The effect:* Sulphur Aria's Strong damage is 11 in a 20-ft radius. Everything in that circle takes 12 fire damage unless it has resistance. The goblins have no armor and no resistance. Four goblins, twelve damage each. The barricade, wooden, dry, catches fire. The goblins' formation collapses into screaming chaos.

*The aftermath:* The Sulphur Aria is per-encounter. Sera won't cast it again this fight. But she doesn't need to. She just cleared the room. Now she draws her dagger and lets the Protector handle cleanup while she looks for her next opening.

That's how magic works in _Heroes of Legend._ No "sorry, I missed." No "I'm out of mana." Just one result and a room full of consequences.
```
